summary:
Section 198 of Brunei's Syariah Penal Code creates the trans-specific offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa". Official guidance on the code states that it binds all persons in the country including tourists, and travel agents are briefed to that effect.

Human Rights Watch's #OUTLAWED global survey places Brunei among at least two countries, with Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex; the only analogue found elsewhere is a state-level sharia provision in a neighbouring jurisdiction.

The US State Department's 2017 report on human rights practices describes the provision as banning men from dressing as women and women from dressing as men "without reasonable excuse", with no known convictions recorded in 2017. Morality provisions covering cross-dressing were among those enforced under the code at that time, while the sharia implementing regulations had not been issued.

One enforcement data point exists: on 11 March 2015 a civil servant was fined B$1,000 under the Syariah Penal Code Order for cross-dressing.

Brunei does not permit a person to change their name or gender marker on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not available. A trans visitor's documents will therefore present the sex assigned at birth, in a jurisdiction where cross-dressing itself is an offence.

The wider code entered its final stage on 3 April 2019, adding death by stoning for anal sex and adultery, amputation for theft, and 40 strokes of the cane for sex between women. These provisions apply principally to Muslims, roughly two-thirds of a population of about 420,000. Brunei has carried out no execution since 1957, and the sultan stated in 2019 that the standing moratorium on capital punishment covers the new provisions; a freshness check in September 2026 confirmed the moratorium intact. Where the sharia evidentiary standards are not met, secular-era fallback penalties apply: sex between men carries up to seven years' imprisonment and 30 strokes of whipping, or one year or 100 lashes for unmarried men, and sex between women any two of 40 lashes, up to 10 years' imprisonment, and a fine of up to B$40,000.

LGBTI people in Brunei report intimidation by police, including threats to publicise a person's sexuality in order to obstruct access to government employment or graduation from government academic institutions. Government monitoring of LGBTI people's activities and communications is reported, and events on LGBTI topics have been refused permits under assembly and expression restrictions.

US State Department reporting records discrimination affecting LGBTI people in employment, housing, recreation and services.
tangentialFactors:
Brunei's regime sits within a narrow group: at least 67 countries criminalise same-sex relations, and at least nine criminalise gender expression in law. Brunei is one of the jurisdictions where the gender-expression offence is written into national statute rather than left to sub-national sharia.

Bruneian society tends to associate homosexuality with "effeminate men", a framing that raises the risk of gender-nonconforming visitors being read through a criminal lens regardless of their stated identity.

The 2019 implementation drew international condemnation. Human Rights Watch called the code "barbaric", the UN High Commissioner urged Brunei to halt it, and the UN urged a review of the laws when the shift to sharia law was announced. International media covering the code described its provisions as "medieval" and "uncivilized". First-person reporting in April 2019 described a climate of fear among LGBTI people, with no assurance that enforcement would exclude foreigners.

OutRight Action International has described Brunei as the country with the most worrisome state of rights for LGBT people in Southeast Asia.
localsOnly:
Brunei's LGBTI community reports sustained government monitoring of its activities and communications. Events on LGBTI topics have been refused permits under assembly and expression restrictions.

Police intimidation tactics reported by LGBTI residents include threats to make a person's sexuality public in order to block government jobs or graduation from government academic institutions.

A civil servant was fined B$1,000 on 11 March 2015 for cross-dressing under the Syariah Penal Code Order, showing the morality provisions reach state employment.

Residents face documented discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and services. Anyone convicted of "tarnishing the image of Islam" may be heavily punished, a charge that can be levelled at public gender nonconformity.

Name and gender marker changes on official documents are not available, and sex reassignment surgery is not permitted, so transition is not legally recognised in any form.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two primary sources could not be retrieved at research time: the hosted text of Brunei's Penal Code including the Syariah provisions returned HTTP 403, and an SSRN paper on the sharia penal code also returned HTTP 403. The wording of section 198 is therefore taken from secondary description rather than the statute text itself, and the official-guidance statement that the offence binds tourists could not be verified against the primary document.

Unresolved: no source in the inventory documents whether section 198 has been applied to a foreign national, or whether entry screening or visa processes ask questions that could disclose a visitor's trans status. The 2015 cross-dressing conviction involved a civil servant, a resident.

The claim that the sharia implementing regulations had not been issued comes from 2017 reporting. Whether they have since been issued is unresolved in this inventory; the September 2026 freshness check covered only the executions moratorium.

Contemporaneous feature reporting from April 2019 concentrates on the effects on gay and lesbian Bruneians. Its value here is the enforcement climate and the assurance, or lack of it, regarding foreign nationals, not trans-specific detail.
